events/hkbp-founded-1861/title: Missionary conference at Sipirok and the beginning of the HKBP
events/hkbp-founded-1861/summary: On 7 October 1861 Rhenish Mission missionaries meeting at Sipirok agreed to work among the Batak of North Sumatra, the date the Huria Kristen Batak Protestan counts as its founding. Ludwig Ingwer Nommensen, arriving in 1862, led the mission into the Silindung valley and Lake Toba region.
events/hkbp-founded-1861/causes/1: Earlier failed missions (e.g. the killing of Lyman and Munson, 1834)
events/hkbp-founded-1861/consequences/0: Mass conversion of the Toba Batak
events/hkbp-founded-1861/consequences/1: Church order granting autonomy (1930) and first Batak ephorus (1940)
events/china-inland-mission-1865/summary: Hudson Taylor founded the China Inland Mission, interdenominational and faith-based, whose missionaries wore Chinese dress and went into all the interior provinces. The Lammermuir party reached Hangzhou in 1866. By 1900 it was the largest Protestant mission in China.
events/first-vatican-council-1870/summar: Pius IX's council defined in Pastor aeternus (18 July 1870) the pope's universal jurisdiction and his infallibility when speaking ex cathedra on faith and morals. A minority left Rome rather than vote no; the council was suspended when Italian troops took Rome. Dissenters in Germany, Switzerland and Austria formed the Old Catholic churches.
events/first-vatican-council-1870/longTe: Vatican I took place amid the loss of the Papal States and the Catholic Church's struggle with liberalism, rationalism and nation-states. The constitution Dei Filius affirmed that God can be known by natural reason and that faith and reason cannot conflict. Pastor aeternus taught that the Roman pontiff, when he defines doctrine ex cathedra, possesses the infallibility Christ willed his church to have, and that such definitions are irreformable 'of themselves, and not from the consent of the church'. Some 60 bishops of the minority, including leading German and French prelates, considered the definition inopportune or historically problematic (the case of Honorius) and left before the final vote. Ignaz von Döllinger refused to accept it and was excommunicated; the Old Catholic churches formed and joined the Union of Utrecht (1889). Orthodox and Protestants saw the definition as the decisive barrier to reunion. Catholic theology since Vatican II has set infallibility within the collegiality of bishops and the sense of the faithful, and only one later definition (1950) is universally regarded as ex cathedra.
events/bulgarian-exarchate-1870/title: Ottoman firman creates the Bulgarian Exarchate
events/bulgarian-exarchate-1870/summary: Under pressure from the Bulgarian national movement, Sultan Abdülaziz issued a firman (1870) creating a Bulgarian Exarchate independent of the Greek-led Patriarchate. A council in Constantinople in 1872 condemned 'ethnophyletism' (organising the church by nationality) and declared the Exarchate schismatic; the schism lasted until 1945.
events/bulgarian-exarchate-1870/causes/0: Bulgarian national revival and resentment of Greek-speaking higher clergy
events/bulgarian-exarchate-1870/conseque: Schism of 1872–1945 between Constantinople and the Bulgarian church
Condemnation of ethnophyletism (1872), still cited in Orthodox ecclesiology
Restoration of a Bulgarian Patriarchate in 1953 (recognised by Constantinople 1961)
events/keswick-convention-1875/summary: In July 1875 Canon T. D. Harford-Battersby hosted the first convention "for the promotion of practical holiness" at Keswick in the English Lake District, following the Higher Life meetings of Robert and Hannah Whitall Smith.
events/keswick-convention-1875/causes/0: Holiness and Higher Life teaching from America
events/keswick-convention-1875/causes/1: Evangelical desire for victorious Christian living
events/keswick-convention-1875/consequen: Annual conventions spread worldwide and shaped evangelical missions spirituality
events/aeterni-patris-1879/title: Leo XIII’s Aeterni Patris revives Thomism
events/aeterni-patris-1879/summary: Leo XIII’s encyclical of 4 August 1879 commended the philosophy of Thomas Aquinas as the model for Catholic schools, launching the neo-Thomist revival and the Leonine critical edition of Aquinas’s works.
events/aeterni-patris-1879/causes/0: Catholic search for a unified response to modern philosophy after Vatican I
events/aeterni-patris-1879/consequences/: Neo-scholastic manuals dominated Catholic seminaries until the 1960s
Provoked, by reaction, the ressourcement movement
events/romanian-autocephaly-1885/title: Constantinople recognises the Romanian Orthodox Church
events/romanian-autocephaly-1885/summary: After the union of Moldavia and Wallachia, Prince Alexandru Ioan Cuza's government asserted the independence of the Romanian church (1865). The Ecumenical Patriarchate granted a Tomos of autocephaly in 1885; the church was raised to a patriarchate in 1925.
events/romanian-autocephaly-1885/causes/: Union of the Romanian principalities (1859) and independence (1878)
Secularisation of monastic estates (1863) and nationalist church reforms
events/uganda-martyrs-1886/summary: Kabaka Mwanga II of Buganda executed Catholic and Anglican pages and courtiers who refused his demands, burning 32 alive at Namugongo on 3 June 1886, among them Charles Lwanga. Their deaths fuelled rapid growth of both churches; the Catholic martyrs were canonised in 1964.
events/uganda-martyrs-1886/causes/0: Political struggle at the Buganda court
events/uganda-martyrs-1886/causes/1: Christians' refusal of the king's sexual demands
events/mar-thoma-separation-1889/title: Royal Court verdict and the formation of the Mar Thoma Church
events/mar-thoma-separation-1889/summary: Reform among the St Thomas Christians, led from 1836 by Abraham Malpan of Maramon and encouraged by contact with Church Missionary Society missionaries, revised the Syriac liturgy to remove prayers for the dead and the invocation of saints. When the Royal Court of Travancore ruled in 1889 that church property belonged to the party loyal to the Syriac patriarch, the reform party continued as the Mar Thoma Syrian Church.
events/mar-thoma-separation-1889/causes/: CMS 'Mission of Help' (from 1816) and the Malayalam Bible
Contest between Mathews Mar Athanasius and the patriarchal party over the metropolitanate
events/mar-thoma-separation-1889/consequ: Mar Thoma Syrian Church as an Oriental-rite church with Reformation emphases
Later communion relations with Anglican churches and the Church of South India
events/rerum-novarum-1891/title: Rerum Novarum and Catholic social teaching
events/rerum-novarum-1891/summary: Leo XIII's encyclical on capital and labour defended private property against socialism while affirming workers' rights to a just wage and to form unions. It launched modern Catholic social teaching, developed by later popes.
events/national-baptist-convention-1895/: Formation of the National Baptist Convention in Atlanta

In September 1895 three African American Baptist bodies — the Foreign Mission Baptist Convention (1880), the American National Baptist Convention (1886) and the Baptist National Educational Convention (1893) — merged in Atlanta to form the National Baptist Convention of the United States of America, the largest Black denomination in the country.
Explosive growth of independent Black Baptist churches after emancipation
Desire for Black-led missions to Africa, publishing and education
Exclusion and paternalism in white-led Baptist bodies
1915 split over control of the publishing board produced the National Baptist Convention of America
1961 split over leadership and civil-rights strategy produced the Progressive National Baptist Convention, the denominational home of Martin Luther King Jr.
Black Baptist churches became central institutions of the civil rights movement
events/pncc-founded-1897/title: Founding of the Polish National Catholic Church
events/pncc-founded-1897/summary: Polish immigrant parishioners in Scranton, at odds with their Irish-American bishop over parish property and Polish-led leadership, organised St Stanislaus parish under Fr Francis Hodur (1897). Hodur was excommunicated in 1898 and consecrated a bishop by Old Catholic bishops in Utrecht in 1907.
events/pncc-founded-1897/causes/0: Trustee and property disputes in immigrant parishes
events/pncc-founded-1897/causes/1: Polish national feeling and resentment of non-Polish hierarchy
events/pncc-founded-1897/consequences/0: Polish National Catholic Church with mission in Poland
events/pncc-founded-1897/consequences/1: Membership of the Old Catholic Union of Utrecht (1907–2003)
events/pncc-founded-1897/consequences/2: Dialogue with the Roman Catholic Church from the 1980s
events/boxer-uprising-1900/summary: The anti-foreign Boxer movement, with Qing support, killed some 32,000 Chinese Catholics, 2,000 Protestants and over 200 missionaries in northern China, notably at Taiyuan in Shanxi. Foreign armies crushed the uprising and imposed indemnities; Chinese Christians' sufferings were later honoured by both Catholics and Protestants.
events/aglipayan-schism-1902/title: Proclamation of the Iglesia Filipina Independiente
events/aglipayan-schism-1902/summary: On 3 August 1902 labour leader Isabelo de los Reyes proclaimed an independent Filipino church at a meeting of the Unión Obrera Democrática, naming the priest Gregorio Aglipay as its head. It arose from nationalist resentment of Spanish friar control during the Philippine Revolution.
events/aglipayan-schism-1902/causes/1: Rome's refusal to appoint Filipino bishops quickly
events/aglipayan-schism-1902/consequence: A large secession of Filipino Catholics in the early 1900s
Supreme Court ruling (1906) returning occupied church buildings to the Catholic Church
Concordat of full communion with the Episcopal Church (1961)
events/welsh-revival-1904/summary: The young ex-miner Evan Roberts led meetings marked by spontaneous prayer, singing and confession, beginning at Loughor in November 1904. Some 100,000 conversions were reported in Wales within months, with reports inspiring revivals in India, Korea and Los Angeles.
events/welsh-revival-1904/consequences/0: Inspiration for Azusa Street and Pyongyang
events/mukti-revival-1905/summary: At Pandita Ramabai's Mukti Mission for widows and orphaned girls, prayer for revival led in 1905 to intense repentance, visions and, by some reports, speaking in tongues. It is often cited as an Indian origin of Pentecostalism independent of North America.
events/mukti-revival-1905/causes/0: Ramabai's prayer bands inspired by Welsh reports
events/churches-of-christ-instrument-div: Churches of Christ listed separately from the Disciples

After decades of dispute over instrumental music and missionary societies (instruments first introduced at Midway, Kentucky, c.1860; Daniel Sommer’s Sand Creek Address, 1889), the US religious census lists the a cappella Churches of Christ separately from the Disciples of Christ.
Restorationist principle of New Testament precedent
Non-instrumental Churches of Christ as a distinct fellowship
events/azusa-street-revival-1906/summary: William J. Seymour, an African American Holiness preacher taught by Charles Parham, led meetings at the Apostolic Faith Mission on Azusa Street from April 1906, where Black, white, Latino and Asian worshippers spoke in tongues and reported healings. Missionaries spread the message within two years to some 50 countries.
events/azusa-street-revival-1906/longTex: Seymour had accepted Parham's teaching that speaking in tongues is the initial evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit, though Parham's segregation forced him to listen from outside the classroom. Invited to Los Angeles, he was locked out of a Holiness church and began meetings in a home on Bonnie Brae Street, where tongues broke out on 9 April 1906; the meetings moved to a former AME building at 312 Azusa Street. Its newspaper, The Apostolic Faith, reached tens of thousands. Visitors noted the interracial character — 'the color line was washed away in the blood' — a striking contrast with Jim Crow America, though racial divisions soon re-emerged, including Parham's own denunciation. Critics mocked the noise and claimed demonic influence; Pentecostals see it as a latter-rain outpouring. Historians stress Azusa's catalytic role while noting parallel revivals in Wales, India (Mukti), Korea and Chile. The Pentecostal and charismatic movements descending from these currents now number hundreds of millions.
